reigns.tagline: The last king crowned at Reims, toppled in three days
reigns.previously: Louis XVIII dies in his bed, the last French king to do so.
paragraphs: As Count of Artois, Charles had been the dashing, spendy young brother at Versailles. He fled in July 1789, days after the Bastille fell, and spent the Revolution leading the émigré hardliners. Crowned at Reims in 1825 with the full medieval ritual, he even touched the sick to cure them, as kings once did.

His government paid compensation to nobles whose lands the Revolution had seized, and made some sacrilege in churches a capital crime. Voters kept sending back liberals. In 1829 he appointed Prince Jules de Polignac, an ultra-royalist, to run the government. In July 1830 news arrived that French troops had taken Algiers.

Feeling strong, Charles issued the July Ordinances: the press muzzled, the new parliament dissolved, fewer voters. Paris threw up barricades. In three days of fighting, from 27 to 29 July, the army lost the city. Charles abdicated on 2 August in favour of his nine-year-old grandson, then sailed for exile in Britain.

claims.text: Charles's son reigned as Louis XIX for about twenty minutes.
claims.note: The Duke of Angoulême held off before signing his own renunciation after his father abdicated. Legitimists sometimes count him as king; nobody in France did at the time.

claims.text: The Bourbons 'learned nothing and forgot nothing'.
claims.note: Usually credited to Talleyrand. Similar lines were going round among émigré-watchers long before, so who said it first is unclear.

claims.text: Charles touched sufferers of scrofula after his coronation.
claims.note: He did it on 31 May 1825 at Reims. Reports at the time give the number touched as over a hundred.

reigns.hook: Paris has thrown out the Bourbons again. Instead of a republic, the deputies turn to a cousin, the Duke of Orléans, whose father voted to kill Louis XVI.

reigns.tagline: The king with the umbrella who ended up as 'Mr Smith'
reigns.previously: Three days of barricades. Charles X abdicates and sails for Britain.
paragraphs: Louis-Philippe had a strange past for a king. His father, Philippe Égalité, voted for Louis XVI's death and was guillotined anyway. The son fought for the Revolution at Valmy, deserted in 1793, and spent years in exile, including a spell teaching in Switzerland and a trip round the young United States.

In 1830 he became King of the French, not of France, and played the bourgeois monarch. He strolled Paris with an umbrella and sent his sons to ordinary schools. Cartoonists drew his head as a pear and were fined for it. Republicans kept trying to kill him; in 1835 a bomb of 25 gun barrels missed him and killed 18 others.

Only rich men could vote, and the king refused to widen it. In February 1848 the government banned a reform banquet in Paris. Crowds rose, troops fired, barricades went up. On 24 February he abdicated for his grandson and slipped away. He crossed to England disguised, travelling as 'Mr Smith', and died there two years later.

claims.text: He fled to England under the name 'Mr Smith'.
claims.note: The British consul at Le Havre arranged his escape on a steamer, and the consul's reports to London describe the disguise.

claims.text: A cartoonist proved in court that the king's face 'was' a pear.
claims.note: Charles Philipon sketched the king's head turning into a pear step by step at his 1831 trial. He was fined anyway, and the pear spread everywhere.

claims.text: The government's motto was 'Enrich yourselves'.
claims.note: François Guizot did say it, but as advice on how to get the vote: enrich yourselves by work and saving. Critics quoted only the first part.

reigns.hook: The king is gone. In Paris, crowds invade the Chamber, and a romantic poet named Lamartine steps forward to proclaim a republic.

reigns.title: The Second Republic
reigns.tagline: Every man gets a vote, and they vote for a Bonaparte
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by its own president's coup
reigns.previously: Louis-Philippe abdicates and slips away to England as 'Mr Smith'.
paragraphs: The new republic moved fast. It gave the vote to every adult man, ended slavery in the colonies and set up National Workshops for the unemployed. When the workshops were shut that June, eastern Paris rose. General Cavaignac crushed the June Days in four days of street fighting. Thousands died and thousands more were deported.

In December 1848 France elected its first president by popular vote. The winner, with about three votes in four, was Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, the late Emperor's nephew. He'd tried two comic-opera coups, been jailed in the fortress of Ham, and escaped in 1846 dressed as a workman. Peasants voted for the name.

The constitution allowed one four-year term, and parliament refused to change it. So on 2 December 1851, the anniversary of Austerlitz, he struck. Troops seized Paris, deputies were arrested and resistance was shot down. Victor Hugo fled into exile. A year later, a vote approved an empire.

claims.text: Lamartine talked the crowd out of adopting the red flag.
claims.note: His speech at the Hôtel de Ville in February 1848 saved the tricolour, and Lamartine retold it proudly himself.

claims.text: Karl Marx said of this coup that history repeats itself, first as tragedy, then as farce.
claims.note: Karl Marx opened The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852) with this jab, comparing the nephew's coup to the uncle's.

claims.text: Louis-Napoleon's nickname 'Badinguet' came from the workman whose clothes he borrowed to escape Ham.
claims.note: Enemies used the name constantly, but there's no solid evidence of a real Badinguet behind it.

reigns.hook: Exactly a year after the coup, the republic is gone. The Prince-President takes his uncle's old title and a new number: Napoleon III.

reigns.tagline: The last emperor rebuilt Paris and lost it all at Sedan
reigns.previously: The Prince-President's coup wins its vote. The republic is dead.
paragraphs: Napoleon III married the Spanish beauty Eugénie de Montijo in 1853 and set out to make France modern. Baron Haussmann tore down old Paris and built the boulevards, parks and sewers you still see. Railways and banks boomed. Abroad he won in Crimea and in Italy, picking up Nice and Savoy for France.

The luck ran out. His plan to put an Austrian archduke on a throne in Mexico ended with Maximilian in front of a firing squad in 1867. Bismarck's Prussia was rising next door. In July 1870, after a doctored telegram from Ems, France declared war. The emperor took command himself, though he was in agony from a bladder stone.

On 2 September 1870, trapped at Sedan, he surrendered with his whole army. Two days later Paris proclaimed a republic, and Eugénie escaped with help from her American dentist. Napoleon died in exile in Kent in 1873. The Third Republic lasted to 1940, and France has never had a monarch since.

claims.text: Bismarck edited the Ems telegram to goad France into war.
claims.note: Bismarck boasted about it in his memoirs. How much it really mattered, given the war fever in Paris, is still argued.

claims.text: Empress Eugénie fled Paris with the help of her American dentist.
claims.note: Dr Thomas Evans wrote his own account of driving her to the coast, and she crossed to England on a British yacht.

claims.text: At Sedan the emperor wore rouge to hide how ill he looked.
claims.note: Some witnesses said so, and he was certainly very sick. It's a detail that suited his enemies, so treat it with care.
